---
title: "Factor Models and Beta Estimation"
metadata:
  pagetitle: "Factor Models and Beta Estimation"
  description-meta: "Estimating alphas, betas and factor loadings in R, and measuring how much of the resulting explanation survives inference."
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/_common.R")
library(tidypm)

ann_ret <- function(x, p = 12) prod(1 + x)^(p / length(x)) - 1
ann_vol <- function(x, p = 12) stats::sd(x) * sqrt(p)
```

@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application described the market one series at a
time. This chapter asks what the series have in common. That question has a
canonical answer, the single-factor model of @sharpe1964, @lintner1965 and
@black1972, in which an asset's expected excess return is proportional to its
covariance with the market. The regression form of it, due to @jensen1968, is
what every risk report still prints: a beta that is the input to a hedge, and an
alpha that is the claim an active manager makes.

We first set out the model and what its components mean, then estimate it on
this market, and then examine how much of the resulting explanation survives
being measured properly. The finding worth stating in advance is that most of it
does not. Outside equity the typical beta changes sign in about a third of all
estimation windows, an apparent asymmetry between rising and falling markets
survives inference in two cases out of sixteen, and a factor that appears to
add explanatory power turns out to be sorting on something other than its name.

## The Single-Factor Model {#sec-05-factor-models-theory}

Write $r_{it}$ for the return on asset $i$ in period $t$, $r_{ft}$ for the
risk-free rate, and $r_{mt}$ for the return on the market. Returns enter in
excess of the bill throughout, for the reasons set out in
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory. The regression is

$$
r_{it} - r_{ft} = \alpha_i + \beta_i\left(r_{mt} - r_{ft}\right) + \varepsilon_{it},
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{it}] = 0,
\quad
\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_{it}, r_{mt}) = 0,
$$ {#eq-05-capm}

with the population slope

$$
\beta_i = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(r_i, r_m)}{\operatorname{Var}(r_m)} .
$$ {#eq-05-beta}

Under the asset pricing theory, $\alpha_i = 0$ for every asset. Under the
regression read as a statistical description, $\alpha_i$ is whatever the market
does not account for, and @eq-05-capm splits the variance of each asset into a
part the market explains and a part it does not:

$$
\underbrace{\operatorname{Var}(r_i)}_{\text{total}}
= \underbrace{\beta_i^2 \operatorname{Var}(r_m)}_{\text{systematic}}
+ \underbrace{\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)}_{\text{idiosyncratic}},
\qquad
R^2_i = \frac{\beta_i^2\operatorname{Var}(r_m)}{\operatorname{Var}(r_i)} .
$$ {#eq-05-variance-split}

The $R^2$ is therefore not a goodness-of-fit statistic in the usual decorative
sense. It is the share of an asset's risk that the model claims to describe, and
an asset with a low $R^2$ is one the model has nothing to say about.

Two extensions matter here. The first allows the slope to differ in rising and
falling markets, in the spirit of the lower partial moment framework of
@bawa1977 and the downside betas of @ang2006:

$$
r_{it} - r_{ft} = \alpha_i + \beta_i\,\tilde{r}_{mt}
  + \gamma_i\,\tilde{r}_{mt}\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{r}_{mt} < 0\} + \varepsilon_{it},
$$ {#eq-05-asymmetric}

where $\tilde{r}_{mt} = r_{mt} - r_{ft}$, so that $\beta_i$ is the beta in up
markets and $\beta_i + \gamma_i$ the beta in down markets. The second allows the
slope to move over time, which is the conditional CAPM of @ferson1991 and
@jagannathan1996 and which we approach here descriptively, through rolling
windows.

### Inference is where these models are usually lost

Monthly returns are serially dependent and heteroskedastic, so the textbook
standard error of an ordinary least squares slope is wrong. Throughout this
chapter we use the heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent estimator
of @newey1987, which replaces $\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}$ with

$$
(X'X)^{-1}\left(\sum_{j=-L}^{L} w_j \hat{\Gamma}_j\right)(X'X)^{-1},
\qquad
w_j = 1 - \frac{|j|}{L+1},
$$ {#eq-05-neweywest}

where $\hat{\Gamma}_j$ is the sample autocovariance of the score at lag $j$ and
$L$ the bandwidth, six lags here.

The reason to insist on this is that @eq-05-asymmetric is estimated sixteen
times, once per series, and any procedure repeated sixteen times will produce
significant-looking differences whether or not any exist. @harvey2016 make the
case at scale for the cross-section of expected returns; the same arithmetic
applies to a table of sixteen betas.

## Implementation {#sec-05-factor-models-implementation}

A factor model needs a factor. The obvious one here is the market, and it has to
be built rather than assumed. We build it from the instrument universe described
in @sec-02-notation-and-data-simulated-market, not from the class series, because
a capitalization weight only exists at instrument level.

```{r}
#| label: proxy
returns <- sim_class_returns_monthly
R  <- as_xts_pm(returns, date, class, return)
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return
risky <- colnames(R)
stopifnot(length(risky) == 16L)

# Capitalization-weighted global equity, from all 123 equity instruments. The
# weight in month t is the last capitalization observed on or before the end of
# t-1: a weight an investor could actually have held.
eq  <- sim_assets$asset_id[sim_assets$asset_class == "equity"]
Ra  <- as_xts_pm(sim_asset_returns_monthly[sim_asset_returns_monthly$asset %in% eq, ],
                 date, asset, return)
cap <- sim_marketcap_weekly[sim_marketcap_weekly$asset %in% eq, ]
d   <- zoo::index(Ra)
stopifnot(ncol(Ra) == 123L, identical(d, zoo::index(R)))

W <- t(vapply(seq_along(d), function(i) {
  cutoff <- if (i == 1) d[1] - 40 else d[i - 1]
  cc   <- cap[cap$date <= cutoff, ]
  last <- cc[!duplicated(cc$asset, fromLast = TRUE), ]
  w <- last$market_cap[match(colnames(Ra), last$asset)]
  w[is.na(w)] <- 0
  if (sum(w) == 0) rep(1 / ncol(Ra), ncol(Ra)) else w / sum(w)
}, numeric(ncol(Ra))))

MKT   <- rowSums(W * zoo::coredata(Ra))
mkt_e <- MKT - rf
```

The weights are lagged by one period deliberately. A capitalization weight
observed at the end of month $t$ is not available for investing during month $t$,
and using it would give the proxy a return no investor could have earned.

```{r}
#| label: proxy-composition
c(annualized = ann_ret(MKT), volatility = ann_vol(MKT))

# Which region is this "global" market, really?
usm <- sim_assets$region[match(colnames(Ra), sim_assets$asset_id)] == "US"
us_share <- rowSums(W[, usm])
c(first = us_share[1], mean = mean(us_share), last = us_share[length(us_share)])
```

The second line deserves attention before any beta in this chapter is used. The
proxy is on average `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(us_share))` United States by
weight and ends the sample at
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * us_share[length(us_share)])`. It is global in
construction and American in effect. Every beta below is largely a beta on the
United States market, and @roll1977 is the standing reminder that a test of
@eq-05-capm is a joint test of the model and of whatever proxy stands in for the
market.

### One factor, sixteen series

```{r}
#| label: single-factor
fit1 <- lapply(colnames(R), function(s) {
  y <- as.numeric(R[, s]) - rf
  m <- stats::lm(y ~ mkt_e)
  nw <- sandwich::NeweyWest(m, lag = 6, prewhite = FALSE)
  tibble::tibble(series = s,
                 alpha_ann = 12 * stats::coef(m)[1],
                 alpha_t   = stats::coef(m)[1] / sqrt(nw[1, 1]),
                 beta      = stats::coef(m)[2],
                 r2        = summary(m)$r.squared)
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-05-single-factor
#| tbl-cap: "One factor. Alphas are annualized; t-statistics use Newey-West standard errors at six lags."
#| echo: false
fit1 |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(r2)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(alpha_ann = sprintf("%+.2f%%", 100 * alpha_ann),
                dplyr::across(c(alpha_t, beta, r2), ~ sprintf("%.3f", .x))) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrr",
               col.names = c("", "alpha", "t(alpha)", "beta", "R²"))
```

Read @tbl-05-single-factor through @eq-05-variance-split. The model explains
`r sum(fit1$r2 > 0.5)` series and fails on the rest. Above an $R^2$ of one half
sit `r paste0("\x60", sort(fit1$series[fit1$r2 > 0.5]), "\x60", collapse = ", ")`.
`JP_equity` reaches `r sprintf("%.3f", fit1$r2[fit1$series == "JP_equity"])`,
`r sum(fit1$r2 < 0.10)` of the `r nrow(fit1)` fall below
`r sprintf("%.2f", 0.10)`, and the extreme is
`r paste0("\x60", fit1$series[which.min(fit1$r2)], "\x60")` at
`r sprintf("%.6f", min(fit1$r2))`, a
regression that accounts for nothing whatsoever.

The median $R^2$ across all `r nrow(fit1)` is
`r sprintf("%.3f", median(fit1$r2))`. A single-factor model is a model of
equities that happens to be applied to everything else.

```{r}
#| label: fig-05-model-fit
#| fig-cap: "How much of each series the market explains. The four bars above one half are equity blocks; everything else is a regression that has not been told what drives it."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.55
stopifnot(sum(fit1$r2 > 0.5) == 4L,                       # the caption says four
          all(grepl("_equity$", fit1$series[fit1$r2 > 0.5])))
fit1 |>
  dplyr::mutate(kind = dplyr::case_when(
    grepl("_equity$", series)     ~ "equity",
    grepl("_credit$", series)     ~ "credit",
    grepl("_government$", series) ~ "government",
    TRUE                          ~ "commodity")) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(stats::reorder(series, r2), r2, fill = kind)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35,
                      colour = tidyaa_colors[["ink_soft"]]) +
  ggplot2::coord_flip() +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    equity = tidyaa_colors[["broken"]], credit = tidyaa_colors[["caution"]],
    government = tidyaa_colors[["blue"]],
    commodity = tidyaa_colors[["good"]])) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "R² on the market factor", fill = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: alpha-claims
#| include: false
# Which alphas clear a t-statistic of two, and which comes next.
by_t      <- fit1[order(-abs(fit1$alpha_t)), ]
sig_alpha <- by_t$series[abs(by_t$alpha_t) > 2]
stopifnot(identical(sig_alpha, "US_government"), by_t$series[2] == "US_credit")
```

Of the `r nrow(fit1)` alphas only one clears a t-statistic of two, that of
`US_government` at
`r sprintf("%+.2f%%", 100 * fit1$alpha_ann[fit1$series == "US_government"])` a
year with t = `r sprintf("%.2f", fit1$alpha_t[fit1$series == "US_government"])`.
`US_credit` comes next, at
`r sprintf("%+.2f%%", 100 * fit1$alpha_ann[fit1$series == "US_credit"])` with
t = `r sprintf("%.2f", fit1$alpha_t[fit1$series == "US_credit"])`, and both
return later. A government bond carrying significant alpha against an equity
market is not a mispricing. It is the model reporting that it has the wrong
factors, exactly as @fama1993 argued when adding a term structure and a default
factor for precisely these assets.

### Splitting the beta, and then testing the split

A single beta assumes @eq-05-beta is the same on the way up and on the way down.
`PerformanceAnalytics` estimates the two halves of @eq-05-asymmetric in one call.

```{r}
#| label: conditional-betas
Rm <- xts::xts(MKT, order.by = d)
rfx <- xts::xts(rf, order.by = d)

cond <- lapply(colnames(R), function(s) {
  tibble::tibble(
    series = s,
    beta   = PerformanceAnalytics::CAPM.beta(R[, s], Rm, rfx),
    bull   = PerformanceAnalytics::CAPM.beta.bull(R[, s], Rm, rfx),
    bear   = PerformanceAnalytics::CAPM.beta.bear(R[, s], Rm, rfx)
  )
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  dplyr::mutate(gap = bear - bull)

cond |> dplyr::arrange(gap) |> head(4)
```

```{r}
#| label: conditional-claims
#| include: false
# The next paragraph reads two opposite signs off this row.
jp <- cond[cond$series == "JP_government", ]
stopifnot(jp$bull > 0, jp$bear < 0)
```

`JP_government` has an unconditional beta of
`r sprintf("%.4f", jp$beta)`, indistinguishable from zero and the sort of
number that files a series under uncorrelated and forgets it. It is not
uncorrelated. It rises with the market when the market rises, at
`r sprintf("%+.3f", jp$bull)`, and rises against it when the market falls, at
`r sprintf("%+.3f", jp$bear)`. The single
number is the average of two opposite behaviors and destroys the only
interesting property of the series.

Now the step that is usually skipped. An apparent asymmetry has to survive a
test, because splitting a sample in two and comparing the halves is a machine for
producing differences.

```{r}
#| label: asymmetry-test
asym <- lapply(colnames(R), function(s) {
  y  <- as.numeric(R[, s]) - rf
  dn <- as.numeric(mkt_e < 0)
  m  <- stats::lm(y ~ mkt_e + I(mkt_e * dn))
  nw <- sandwich::NeweyWest(m, lag = 6, prewhite = FALSE)
  tibble::tibble(series = s,
                 gap = stats::coef(m)[3],
                 t   = stats::coef(m)[3] / sqrt(nw[3, 3]),
                 p   = 2 * stats::pnorm(-abs(stats::coef(m)[3] / sqrt(nw[3, 3]))))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()

asym |> dplyr::filter(p < 0.05) |> dplyr::arrange(p)
```

```{r}
#| label: asymmetry-claims
#| include: false
# The opening of the chapter states the count; the text here names who survives.
survive <- asym$series[asym$p < 0.05]
stopifnot(length(survive) == 2L, all(grepl("_government$", survive)),
          "JP_government" %in% survive, !"US_credit" %in% survive)
```

This is @eq-05-asymmetric with the standard errors of @eq-05-neweywest, and
`r length(survive)` of `r nrow(asym)` survive, both of them government bonds.
The Japanese bond asymmetry is
real, at t = `r sprintf("%.2f", asym$t[asym$series == "JP_government"])`. The
credit asymmetry, which is the one an allocator would most like to believe in, is
not: `US_credit` has a gap of
`r sprintf("%+.3f", asym$gap[asym$series == "US_credit"])` with
t = `r sprintf("%.2f", asym$t[asym$series == "US_credit"])` and
p = `r sprintf("%.2f", asym$p[asym$series == "US_credit"])`.

There are `r sum(mkt_e < 0)` down months in this sample. Estimating a separate
beta on them, for sixteen series, will produce differences whether or not any
exist. Report the split as a diagnostic; do not build a hedge on it without the
test.

```{r}
#| label: fig-05-asymmetric
#| fig-cap: "Beta when the market rises against beta when it falls. Points below the diagonal fall less than they rise; points above it fall more. Only the filled points survive a Newey-West test of the difference; the rest of the spread is what splitting 372 months into two piles will produce on its own."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.62
cond |>
  dplyr::left_join(dplyr::select(asym, series, p), by = "series") |>
  dplyr::mutate(sig = p < 0.05) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(bull, bear)) +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "22",
                       colour = tidyaa_colors[["ink_soft"]], linewidth = 0.35) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.25,
                      colour = tidyaa_colors[["rule"]]) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(fill = sig), shape = 21, size = 2.8,
                      colour = tidyaa_colors[["ink"]], stroke = 0.6) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = series), size = 2.4, hjust = -0.12,
                     colour = tidyaa_colors[["ink_soft"]]) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = tidyaa_colors[["broken"]],
                                        `FALSE` = "white"), guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0.06, 0.28))) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "beta when the market is up", y = "beta when the market is down")
```

### What a factor is actually sorting on

Size is the second factor everyone reaches for, following @fama1992 and
@fama1993, and here it is a trap worth walking into deliberately.

```{r}
#| label: smb
capW <- W
reg  <- sim_assets$region[match(colnames(Ra), sim_assets$asset_id)]

# Global sort: bottom half by capitalization minus top half.
smb_global <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(Ra)), function(i) {
  w <- capW[i, ]; ok <- w > 0; med <- median(w[ok])
  mean(zoo::coredata(Ra)[i, ok & w <= med]) - mean(zoo::coredata(Ra)[i, ok & w > med])
}, numeric(1))

# Region-neutral: rank within each region, then average the five spreads.
smb_neutral <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(Ra)), function(i) {
  w <- capW[i, ]
  mean(vapply(unique(reg), function(g) {
    j <- reg == g & w > 0; med <- median(w[j])
    mean(zoo::coredata(Ra)[i, j & w <= med]) - mean(zoo::coredata(Ra)[i, j & w > med])
  }, numeric(1)))
}, numeric(1))
```

Before using either, look at what the global sort placed in each leg.

```{r}
#| label: smb-legs
legs <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(Ra)), function(i) {
  w <- capW[i, ]; ok <- w > 0; med <- median(w[ok])
  c(big_us   = sum(w[ok & w > med & reg[ok] == "US"]) / sum(w[ok & w > med]),
    small_us = sum(w[ok & w <= med & reg[ok] == "US"]) / sum(w[ok & w <= med]))
}, numeric(2))
round(rowMeans(legs), 3)
```

The big leg is `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(legs["big_us", ]))` United States.
The small leg is `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(legs["small_us", ]))`. A global
capitalization sort in a five-region universe does not sort on size. It sorts on
region, and since region carries a currency, it sorts on currency too.

The consequence is measurable.

```{r}
#| label: smb-r2
med_r2 <- function(f = NULL) {
  median(vapply(risky, function(s) {
    y <- as.numeric(R[, s]) - rf
    summary(if (is.null(f)) stats::lm(y ~ mkt_e) else stats::lm(y ~ mkt_e + f))$r.squared
  }, numeric(1)))
}
c(market_only  = med_r2(),
  plus_global  = med_r2(smb_global),
  plus_neutral = med_r2(smb_neutral))

# The premium of each construction, with its Newey-West t-statistic.
nw_t <- function(x) {
  m <- stats::lm(x ~ 1)
  unname(stats::coef(m)[1] / sqrt(sandwich::NeweyWest(m, lag = 6, prewhite = FALSE)[1, 1]))
}
c(global_premium  = ann_ret(smb_global),  global_t  = nw_t(smb_global),
  neutral_premium = ann_ret(smb_neutral), neutral_t = nw_t(smb_neutral),
  correlation     = cor(smb_global, smb_neutral))
```

```{r}
#| label: smb-claims
#| include: false
# The two orders the next paragraphs state.
stopifnot(med_r2(smb_global) > med_r2(smb_neutral), med_r2(smb_neutral) > med_r2(),
          nw_t(smb_neutral) > 2, nw_t(smb_neutral) > nw_t(smb_global))
```

Adding the global size factor lifts the median $R^2$ from
`r sprintf("%.3f", med_r2())` to `r sprintf("%.3f", med_r2(smb_global))`.
Constructing the same factor region-neutrally lifts it only to
`r sprintf("%.3f", med_r2(smb_neutral))`, an improvement of
`r sprintf("%.3f", med_r2(smb_neutral) - med_r2())`. The explanatory power was
not size. It was the regional composition of the legs.

The premium runs the other way. The region-neutral factor earns
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * ann_ret(smb_neutral))` a year with a t-statistic of
`r sprintf("%.2f", nw_t(smb_neutral))`, the global sort
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * ann_ret(smb_global))` with
`r sprintf("%.2f", nw_t(smb_global))`: the construction that explains less
variance carries the more reliable premium. The lesson is not
that size does not exist. It is that a factor is defined by its construction, and
a sort nobody has inspected is a bet nobody has chosen. @griffin2002 makes the
empirical case that the size and value factors are country-specific rather than
global, and @hou2011 reach a similar conclusion on a wider cross-section. A
practitioner building a global factor without neutralizing the country dimension
is, on this evidence, building a country factor.

::: {.callout-note}
## `table.CAPM()` computes most of this chapter in one call

`PerformanceAnalytics::table.CAPM()` returns alpha and beta with their p-values,
the bull and bear betas, $R^2$, tracking error, the information ratio, Treynor's
ratio and the appraisal ratio, for as many series as it is handed. Most readers
compute these one function at a time, and several never learn that the
conditional betas are in there.
:::

```{r}
#| label: table-capm
PerformanceAnalytics::table.CAPM(R[, c("US_credit", "JP_government", "US_equity")],
                                 Rm, Rf = rfx)
```

Use it for the survey and the individual functions for the argument. The table
reports no standard error on the bull-minus-bear gap, which is the number that
decides whether the split means anything.

## How Much of This Survives {#sec-05-factor-models-application}

### A beta is a time series

@eq-05-beta is written as though $\beta_i$ were a constant. The conditional asset
pricing literature starting with @ferson1991 and @jagannathan1996 assumes it is
not, and a rolling window shows directly how much it moves.

```{r}
#| label: rolling-betas
win <- 60L
roll_beta <- function(s) {
  y <- as.numeric(R[, s]) - rf
  zoo::rollapply(cbind(y, mkt_e), win,
                 function(z) stats::cov(z[, 1], z[, 2]) / stats::var(z[, 2]),
                 by.column = FALSE, align = "right")
}

travel <- lapply(risky, function(s) {
  b <- roll_beta(s)
  tibble::tibble(series = s,
                 full = stats::cov(as.numeric(R[, s]) - rf, mkt_e) / stats::var(mkt_e),
                 min = min(b), max = max(b), travel = diff(range(b)),
                 sign_flips = mean(sign(b) != sign(stats::cov(as.numeric(R[, s]) - rf, mkt_e))))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows() |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(travel))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-05-rolling
#| tbl-cap: "Sixty-month rolling betas against the same proxy. `travel` is the distance from the lowest window to the highest; `sign_flips` is the share of windows whose beta disagrees in sign with the full-sample estimate."
#| echo: false
travel |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(full, min, max, travel), ~ sprintf("%+.3f", .x)),
                sign_flips = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * sign_flips)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrr",
               col.names = c("", "full sample", "lowest", "highest", "travel", "sign flips"))
```

```{r}
#| label: rolling-claims
#| include: false
# The orders and signs the next two paragraphs, and the opening, state.
flips  <- stats::setNames(travel$sign_flips, travel$series)
is_eq  <- grepl("_equity$", names(flips))
flip_p <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
stopifnot(
  !is_eq[1], abs(travel$full[1]) < 0.5,            # the furthest traveler is a small beta
  all(flips[is_eq] == 0), all(flips[!is_eq] > 0),  # equity never flips, the rest all do
  names(which.max(flips)) == "JP_government",
  travel$series[which.min(abs(travel$full))] == "JP_government",
  names(which.min(flips[!is_eq])) == "US_government", travel$full[travel$series == "US_government"] < 0,
  abs(median(flips[!is_eq]) - 1 / 3) < 0.05        # "about a third", in the opening
)
```

Two patterns emerge, and the second is the one to carry forward.

The betas that travel furthest are not the largest.
`r paste0("\x60", travel$series[1], "\x60")` moves
`r sprintf("%.2f", travel$travel[1])` across the sample, from
`r sprintf("%+.2f", travel$min[1])` to `r sprintf("%+.2f", travel$max[1])`, while
`US_equity`, with a beta near one, travels only
`r sprintf("%.2f", travel$travel[travel$series == "US_equity"])` and never
changes sign. @blume1971 documented the same regularity in individual stocks:
extreme betas are the unreliable ones, and they revert.

The largest full-sample beta outside equity is
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(travel$full[!is_eq])))` in absolute value, and every
one of the `r sum(!is_eq)` changes sign, the median in
`r flip_p(median(flips[!is_eq]))` of all windows. `JP_government`, whose beta is
closest to zero, does so in `r flip_p(flips[["JP_government"]])` and `US_credit`
in `r flip_p(flips[["US_credit"]])`; `US_government`, at
`r flip_p(flips[["US_government"]])`, is the one small beta that is reliably
negative. The five equity series flip in none.

```{r}
#| label: fig-05-rolling-betas
#| fig-cap: "Sixty-month rolling betas for six series. The dashed line is the full-sample estimate. An equity beta moves without changing sign; a beta near zero crosses it repeatedly, which means the sign of the hedge it implies is not known."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.5
show <- c("US_equity", "EU_equity", "US_credit",
          "US_government", "JP_government", "GLOBAL_commodity")
lapply(show, function(s) {
  b <- roll_beta(s)
  tibble::tibble(series = s,
                 date = zoo::index(R)[win:nrow(R)],
                 beta = as.numeric(b))
}) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  dplyr::mutate(series = factor(series, levels = show)) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(date, beta)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.25,
                      colour = tidyaa_colors[["rule"]]) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(data = travel |> dplyr::filter(series %in% show) |>
                        dplyr::mutate(series = factor(series, levels = show)),
                      ggplot2::aes(yintercept = full), linetype = "22",
                      linewidth = 0.35, colour = tidyaa_colors[["broken"]]) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = tidyaa_colors[["blue"]], linewidth = 0.5) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ series, nrow = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_model(by = 10) +
  ggplot2::labs(y = NULL)
```

A small beta is not a stable beta. It is a beta whose sign is unknown. That is
why @sec-08-estimation-error-theory exists, and why a hedge ratio needs an error
bar before it needs a decimal place.

### Measuring the instability itself

If the moments move, the movement is itself a quantity. A turbulence index
measures it as the Mahalanobis distance of a period's returns from their recent
mean, scaled by the covariance structure,

$$
d_t = \left(\boldsymbol{r}_t - \boldsymbol{\mu}\right)'
      \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}
      \left(\boldsymbol{r}_t - \boldsymbol{\mu}\right),
$$ {#eq-05-turbulence}

so that an unusual *pattern* of returns counts as turbulent even when no single
series is extreme. @chow1999 introduced the construction for portfolio work and
@kritzman2010 developed it as a risk-management signal. The implementation used
here is @stoeckl-uncertaintymeasures, which is not on CRAN; see
@sec-93-package-notes.

```{r}
#| label: turbulence
library(uncertaintymeasures)

R_risky <- R[, risky]
turb <- OSturbulence(R_risky, rolling = TRUE, roll.obs = 60)
```

`OSturbulence()` estimates $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ from data
strictly before each observation, so the index never sees the month it is
scoring. An in-sample variant exists, and the gap between them is a clean picture
of what look-ahead buys.

```{r}
#| label: turbulence-peaks
tb  <- as.numeric(turb$turb)
top <- order(tb, decreasing = TRUE, na.last = NA)[1:5]

# Which of the named episodes, if any, each month belongs to.
episode_of <- rep("none", length(d))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(sim_episodes))) {
  episode_of[in_episode(d, sim_episodes$episode[i])] <- sim_episodes$label[i]
}

data.frame(month = fmt_model(d[top]), turbulence = round(tb[top], 2),
           episode = episode_of[top])
```

```{r}
#| label: turbulence-claims
#| include: false
# The peak lies in the credit crisis, and it is the month chapter 4 found by
# counting exceedances beyond 2.5 standard deviations.
peak <- which.max(tb)
stopifnot(identical(zoo::index(R_risky), d), peak == top[1],
          in_episode(d[peak], "credit_crisis"),
          peak == which.max(rowSums(abs(scale(R_risky)) > 2.5)))
```

The highest reading in the sample is `r fmt_model(d[peak])`, in the
`r episode_of[peak]`, at `r sprintf("%.2f", tb[peak])`,
`r sprintf("%.2f", tb[top[1]] / tb[top[2]])` times the next one, and
`r sum(episode_of[top] == episode_of[peak])` of the `r length(top)` highest
readings fall in that episode. The peak is the same month
@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application identified by counting
exceedances, arrived at independently, expressed as one number rather than a
count, and available on the day rather than in hindsight.

The component that makes @eq-05-turbulence more than a volatility measure is the
ratio of the full distance to the one computed from variances alone.

```{r}
#| label: correlation-turbulence
ct <- as.numeric(turb$cturb)
c(median     = median(ct, na.rm = TRUE),
  peak_month = ct[peak],
  max        = max(ct, na.rm = TRUE))
```

```{r}
#| label: correlation-turbulence-claims
#| include: false
# "Ordinary" below means inside the interquartile range of the ratio.
stopifnot(ct[peak] > stats::quantile(ct, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
          ct[peak] < stats::quantile(ct, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE))
```

This isolates how much of a turbulent month is correlations breaking rather than
volatilities rising, which is the distinction @forbes2002 showed is easy to
confuse. In the peak month the ratio is `r sprintf("%.2f", ct[peak])` against a
median of `r sprintf("%.2f", median(ct, na.rm = TRUE))`: the most turbulent
month of the sample was a month of extreme moves in an ordinary correlation
structure. @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application found average pairwise
correlation higher in the credit crisis than in calm months, but only by
choosing the windows by hand and knowing the answer first. This is the same
question asked continuously and without hindsight, and it is what a
regime-aware allocation in @sec-19-regimes-theory would have to react to.

```{r}
#| label: fig-05-turbulence
#| fig-cap: "Out-of-sample turbulence, estimated from a sixty-month trailing window. The first five model years are consumed by the window and are not shown."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.42
tibble::tibble(date = zoo::index(R_risky), turbulence = tb) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(turbulence)) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(date, turbulence)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = tidyaa_colors[["blue"]], linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_x_model() +
  ggplot2::labs(y = NULL)
```

## Key Takeaways {.unnumbered}

- The $R^2$ of @eq-05-capm is not decoration. By @eq-05-variance-split it is the
  share of an asset's risk the model claims to describe, and the median across
  these sixteen series is `r sprintf("%.2f", median(fit1$r2))`. A one-factor
  model is an equity model applied to everything else.
- A market proxy has a composition, and this one is on average
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(us_share))` United States and
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * us_share[length(us_share)])` at the end of the
  sample. Every beta computed against it is largely a United States beta
  [@roll1977].
- Conditional betas are worth computing and are rarely worth believing. Of
  sixteen asymmetries estimated with @eq-05-asymmetric, `r length(survive)`
  survive Newey-West inference, and the one an allocator would most want is not
  among them.
- A factor is defined by its construction. A global size sort in a multi-region
  universe puts `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(legs["big_us", ]))` United
  States in one leg and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(legs["small_us", ]))` in
  the other, so it is a region bet wearing a size label [@griffin2002; @hou2011].
- Betas move. Equity betas do so without changing sign; outside equity the
  median beta has the wrong sign in `r flip_p(median(flips[!is_eq]))` of all
  sixty-month windows and the one closest to zero in
  `r flip_p(flips[["JP_government"]])` [@blume1971].
- The instability is itself measurable without hindsight. The Mahalanobis
  turbulence of @eq-05-turbulence picks out `r fmt_model(d[peak])`, in the
  `r episode_of[peak]`, from a trailing window, and its correlation component
  separates dependence breaking down from volatility merely rising [@chow1999;
  @kritzman2010].

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Rebuild the market proxy with equal rather than capitalization weights. Which
   betas move most, and does the ranking in @tbl-05-rolling survive? Explain what
   that says about the phrase "the market".
2. The asymmetry test uses a single interaction term. Replace it with separate
   regressions on the up and down months, and confirm that the point estimates
   agree while the standard errors do not. Which is the honest one, and why?
3. Take the two series with the highest `sign_flips` in @tbl-05-rolling and plot
   their rolling betas against the turbulence index. Does the beta move because
   the market is turbulent, or independently of it?
4. `OSturbulence()` has an `s.k` argument controlling the length of the short
   window whose mean is compared with the long-run mean. Vary it from 1 to 12 and
   describe what the index measures at each end.
5. @harvey2016 argue that a t-statistic of two is too low a bar once many
   hypotheses have been tested. Sixteen asymmetries were tested here. Apply a
   Bonferroni correction and a Benjamini-Hochberg correction to the p-values in
   `asym`, and report how many survive each.
